A.explanation: This is $40.0 \times 305/330$ kHz, the frequency for a source moving away at $25.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, not towards the fixed detector.

B.explanation: This uses $330/(330+25.0)$ so divides by the increased wavelength factor, giving the lower receding-source frequency instead of the higher approaching frequency.

C.explanation: This uses $(330+25.0)/330$, which is the moving-observer formula, not the moving-source formula with $330-25.0$ in the denominator.

D.explanation: Moving source towards stationary observer gives $f_o = 40.0 \times 330/(330-25.0) = 43.3$ kHz, higher than the emitted $40.0$ kHz.

hints: Notice the bat is the moving source at $25.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ towards the fixed detector, so successive $40.0$ kHz wavefronts are crowded together in front of the bat.
For sound with speed $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, the observed wavelength is shortened to $(v - v_s)/f_s$, so the observed frequency must use $f_o = v f_s/(v - v_s)$.
Calculate $330 - 25.0 = 305 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ in the denominator, then multiply $40.0$ kHz by $330/305$ and check whether the result must be above $40.0$ kHz.
walkthrough: Identify the situation: source speed $v_s = 25.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ towards a stationary observer, emitted frequency $f_s = 40.0$ kHz, wave speed $v = 330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
State the Doppler rule for a source approaching a stationary observer: observed wavelength $\lambda_o = (v - v_s)/f_s$ is shorter, so observed frequency $f_o = v/\lambda_o = f_s \times v/(v - v_s)$.
Do the intermediate step: $330 - 25.0 = 305$, so factor $= 330/305 = 1.08197$.
Multiply: $40.0 \times 1.08197 = 43.28$ kHz, which to three significant figures is $43.3$ kHz with increased frequency as expected for approach. This is option D.
